new_apostolic.continuing_revelation:
The New Apostolic Church teaches that Jesus Christ has continued to send apostles to his church, just as he did in the New Testament, and that this continuing apostleship is how he guides and builds up his people today. The apostles are understood to serve as his ambassadors, proclaiming the gospel, teaching, and caring for the unity of the church.

Members do not understand this as adding new books to Scripture. The Bible remains the foundation, and the apostles' role is to interpret and apply it, and to lead the church in obedience to Christ. The conviction is that the risen Lord still directs his church through the office he instituted, and that the apostolic ministry did not end with the first generation. Other churches which regard the apostolic office as closed understand this differently.
new_apostolic.prophetic_authority:
In the New Apostolic Church, the Chief Apostle is the head of the apostle ministry worldwide. Members understand this office as the ministry through which Christ preserves the unity of the church, and the other apostles as the Chief Apostle's co-workers who serve in various regions.

The Chief Apostle is not regarded as sinless or as a source of new Scripture. He is understood as the one entrusted with guiding the church's teaching and care, and members honor him as Christ's representative in that task. Church life is organized around this shared apostolic ministry, and members pray for the Chief Apostle regularly. Other Christians who have no equivalent office may find this unfamiliar, and members generally explain it in terms of unity and service.
new_apostolic.apostles_today:
New Apostolic Christians believe that Christ still calls and sends apostles, and that these men hold the same kind of office as the apostles of the New Testament. Their tasks are to proclaim the gospel, to announce forgiveness of sins in the name of Jesus, and to preside over the sacraments and the ordaining of ministers.

The church names three sacraments: Holy Baptism with water, Holy Communion and Holy Sealing, in which the gift of the Holy Spirit is conveyed through an apostle. Members regard the apostles as servants of Christ and of the congregation, not as rulers, and the office as a means by which the Lord continues to work among his people. Churches that consider the apostolic age closed do not share this understanding, and members are used to explaining it.
